summary: Defines a common framework and XML format for writing rules about who may see application-specific data, such as a person's location or presence. Other documents can extend the rule language for their own needs.

plainLanguage.summary: This document gives a single XML format for writing privacy rules. Each rule says who is asking, what state the person is in, and how long the rule lasts, and then says what may be revealed and how precisely. Other documents can add their own rule elements to it.

subtitle: A shared XML format for rules about who may see your presence or location, built to be extended.

tldr.problem: Systems that expose a person's location or presence each need their own way of writing the rules about who may see that information, and those ways rarely match.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a common framework of rules with three parts: conditions that must hold, actions that permit an operation, and transformations that reduce what is revealed. An XML schema fixes the language, and extensions add domain-specific elements in their own namespaces.
tldr.outcome: Presence and location policies can be written in one format and extended by other documents, with a defined way of combining the permissions from every rule that matches a request.

today: RFC 4745 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document is a work item of the IETF GEOPRIV working group and defines a framework that other documents, such as the presence and location policy extensions, build on.

sections.title: One Format for Privacy Rules
sections.content:
The document defines a framework for creating authorization policies for access to application-specific data. It is the result of combining the common aspects of single authorization systems that more specifically control access to presence and location information and that had previously been developed separately. The benefit of combining them is two-fold: it allows building a system that enhances the value of presence with location information in a natural way and reuses the same underlying authorization mechanism, and it encourages a more generic authorization framework with mechanisms for extensibility. The applicability of the framework is not limited to policies controlling access to presence and location information, and it can be extended to other application domains.

The framework is intended to be accompanied and enhanced by application-specific policies specified elsewhere. The common policy framework is enhanced by domain-specific policy documents, including presence and location, and Figure 1 shows the relationship: the common policy sits above and enhances both a location-specific policy and a presence-specific policy.

The document sets out the terminology, the basic modes of operation, the goals and non-goals of the framework, the data model, the structure of a rule, the procedure for combining permissions, a description of meta policies, an example, the XML schema, and finally the security and IANA considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of system, one for location and one for presence, each grew its own rule language. This document merges the parts they share into one format that other kinds of data can also use.

sections.title: The Roles in a Policy System
sections.content:
The document introduces four roles. The PT, the Presentity or Target, is the entity about whom information has been requested. The RM, the Rule Maker, is the entity that creates the authorization rules that restrict access to data items. The PS, the Authorization Policy Server, has access to both the authorization policies and the data items; in location-specific applications the PS is labeled the location server. The WR, the Watcher or Recipient, requests access to data items of the PT, and an access operation might be a read, a write or any other operation.

A policy is given by a rule set that contains an unordered list of rules. A rule has a conditions part, an actions part and a transformations part. The term permission indicates the action and transformation components of a rule. The using protocol is the protocol used to request access to and return privacy-sensitive data items.
sections.plainLanguage: Four parties: the person the information is about, the one who writes the rules, the server that holds both the rules and the data, and the one asking for the data.

sections.title: How a Request Is Handled
sections.content:
The abstract sequence of operations runs as follows. The PS receives a query for data items for a particular PT, via the using protocol. The using protocol, or more precisely the authentication protocol, provides the identity of the requestor, either at the time of the query or at subscription time. The authenticated identity of the WR, together with other information provided by the using protocol or generally available to the server, is then used for searching through the rule set. All matching rules are combined according to a permission combining algorithm. The combined rules are applied to the application data, resulting in the application of privacy based on the transformation policies, and the resulting application data is returned to the WR.

Three modes of operation are distinguished. In a passive request-response mode, the WR queries the PS for data items about the PT; examples include HTTP, FTP, LDAP, finger and various RPC protocols. The PS uses the rule set to determine whether the WR is authorized to access the PT's information, refusing the request if necessary, and might filter information by removing elements or reducing the resolution of elements.

In an active request-response mode, the PS contacts the WR and conveys data items; examples include HTTP, SIP session setup with an INVITE request, H.323 session setup and SMTP.

Event notification adds a subscription phase to the active mode. A watcher or subscriber asks to be added to the notification list for a particular presentity or event, and when the presentity changes state or the event occurs, the PS sends a message to the WR containing the updated state. Presence is a special case of event notification, so the terms are often used interchangeably. The subscriber may itself add a filter to the subscription, limiting the rate or content of the notifications. If an event, after filtering by the rule-maker-provided rules and by the subscriber-provided rules, only produces the same notification content that was sent previously, no event notification is sent.

A single PS may authorize access to data items in more than one mode. Rather than having different rule sets for different modes, all three modes are supported with one rule set schema, and specific instances of the rule set can omit elements that are only applicable to the subscription model.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks the requester against every rule, works out what the matching rules allow, uses that as a mask over the real data, and sends back what the mask lets through. The same rule set works whether the requester pulls the data or the server pushes it.

sections.title: Design Goals and Non-Goals
sections.content:
The design goals are stated as a series of constraints. Table representation: each rule must be representable as a row in a relational database, so that policy implementation can use standard database optimisation techniques. Permit only: rules only provide permissions rather than denying them, so removing a rule can never increase permissions. Because the ordering of rules might otherwise matter depending on the interpretation of deny and permit rules, making rule updates more complicated and distributed rule sets more complicated, only permit actions are allowed, which also implies that rule ordering is not important and that making a policy decision requires processing all rules.

Additive permissions: a query for access to data items is matched against the rules in the rule database, and if several rules match, the overall permissions granted to the WR are the union of those permissions. Upgradeable: it should be possible to add rules later without breaking servers that have not been upgraded, and such upgrades must not degrade privacy constraints, though un-upgraded servers may reveal less information than the rule maker would have chosen. Capability support: a rule maker should be able to determine which extensions are supported by the PS, though the mechanism for doing so is out of scope. Protocol-independent: the rule set supports constraints on notifications and queries as well as subscriptions for event-based systems. No false assurance: it appears more dangerous to give the user the impression that the system will prevent disclosure automatically but fail to do so with a significant probability of operator error or misunderstanding, than to force the user to invoke simpler rules explicitly. Rules based on weekday and time-of-day ranges seem particularly subject to misinterpretation.

The non-goals are equally explicit. No external references: attributes within specific rules cannot refer to external rule sets, databases, directories or other network elements, because any such external reference would make simple database implementation difficult. No regular expressions: conditions are matched on equality or greater-than style comparisons, not regular expressions, partial matches such as the SQL LIKE operator, or glob-style matches. No repeat times: repeat times such as every day from 9 am to 4 pm are difficult to make work correctly, due to the different time zones the PT, WR, PS and RM may occupy. This feature must not be confused with the Validity element, which restricts the lifetime of a rule.
sections.plainLanguage: The format is deliberately simple so that a server can store it in a database and check it quickly. It only grants access, never denies it, so deleting a rule can only make things more private. And it leaves out patterns and repeating time windows, because those are easy to get subtly wrong.

sections.title: The Rule Set and Its Parts
sections.content:
A rule set, synonymously a policy, consists of zero or more rules, and the ordering of these rules is irrelevant. The rule set can be stored at the PS and conveyed from the rule maker to the PS as a single document, in subsets or as individual rules. A rule consists of three parts: conditions, actions and transformations.

The conditions part is a set of expressions, each of which evaluates to either TRUE or FALSE. When a WR asks for information about a PT, the PS goes through each rule in the rule set and evaluates the expressions in the conditions part. If all of the expressions evaluate to TRUE, the rule is applicable to this request. Generally, each expression specifies a condition based on some variable associated with the context of the request, and these variables can include the identity of the WR, the domain of the WR, the time of day, or even external variables such as the temperature or the mood of the PT.

Assuming the rule is applicable, the actions and transformations, commonly referred to as permissions, specify how the PS is supposed to handle the request. If the request is to view the location or presence of the PT, the typical action is permit, which allows the request to proceed. Assuming the action allows the request to proceed, the transformations part specifies how the information about the PT is modified before being presented to the WR. These transformations are in the form of positive permissions: they always specify a piece of information that is allowed to be seen by the WR. When a PS processes a request, it takes the transformations specified across all rules that match and creates the union of them. For computing this union, the data type, such as Integer, Boolean, Set or the Undef data type, plays a role.

The resulting union effectively represents a mask, defining what information is exposed to the WR. This mask is applied to the actual location or presence data for the PT, and the data permitted by the mask is shown to the WR. If the WR requests only a subset of information, such as city-level civic location data only instead of the full civic location information, the information delivered to the WR MUST be the intersection of the permissions granted to the WR and the data requested by the WR.

Rules are encoded in XML, and the XML schema defines the Common Policy Markup Language. This is purely an exchange format between the rule maker and the policy server; the format does not imply that either uses it internally. The rules are designed so that a PS can translate them into a relational database table, with each rule represented by one row. The database model is by no means mandatory, and smaller-scale implementations may choose a simple traversal of the set of rules.

Each rule is equipped with a parameter that identifies it. This rule identifier is an opaque token chosen by the rule maker, and a rule maker MUST NOT use the same identifier for two rules that are available to the PS at the same time for a given PT. If more than one rule maker modifies the same rule set, a unique identifier has to be ensured for each rule, which the rule maker can do by retrieving the already specified rule set and choosing a new identifier for a rule that is different from the existing rule set.
sections.plainLanguage: A rule has an if part and a then part. The if part is a list of tests that are each true or false. The then part says what the server may do and how much detail it may reveal. The revealed detail works like a mask laid over the real data.

sections.title: The Condition Elements
sections.content:
Each instance of a request has different attributes, such as the identity of the requestor, that are used for authorization. A rule may have a number of conditions that need to be met before executing the rest of the rule. The document specifies only a few conditions: identity, sphere and validity. Further condition elements can be added via extensions. If a child element of the conditions element is in a namespace that is not known or not supported, that child element evaluates to FALSE.

Conditions are matched on equality or greater-than style comparisons rather than regular expressions. Equality is determined according to the rules for the data type associated with the element in the schema, unless explicit comparison steps are included in the document.

The identity condition restricts matching of a rule either to a single entity or a group of entities. Only authenticated entities can be matched, and the acceptable means of authentication are defined in protocol-specific documents. If the identity element is absent, identities are not considered, and other conditions in the rule apply to any user, authenticated or not. The identity condition is TRUE if any of its child elements evaluate to TRUE, so the results of the individual child elements are combined using a logical OR.

The one element matches the authenticated identity of exactly one entity or user. The many element is a mechanism for performing authorization decisions based on the domain part of the authenticated identity, and it allows matching a large and possibly unknown number of users within a domain. One or more except elements can exclude individual users, with except id="..." excluding a particular user, or users belonging to a specific domain, with except domain="...". When multiple except elements are listed, the result of each is combined using a logical OR. A many element with no children matches any authenticated user; one enclosing except domain elements matches any user from any domain except those enumerated; and one with a domain attribute and zero or more except id elements matches any authenticated user from the indicated domain except those enumerated.

Common policy MUST either use UTF-8 or UTF-16 to store domain names in the domain attribute, and for non-internationalized domain names lowercase ASCII SHOULD be used. For the comparison between the stored value and the domain value provided via the using protocol, three steps apply: translate percent-encoding for either string, convert both domain strings using the ToASCII operation described in RFC 3490, and compare the two domain strings for ASCII equality, label by label. If the conversion fails, the domains are not equal.

The sphere element indicates a state, for example work, home, meeting or travel, that the PT is currently in. A sphere condition matches only if the PT is currently in the state indicated, and the state may be conveyed by manual configuration or by some protocol. Switching from one sphere to another causes a switch between different modes of visibility, so different subsets of rules might be applicable. The value attribute may contain more than one token, separated by blank characters, and a logical OR is used for matching the tokens. A case-insensitive string comparison MUST be used for each individual token. There is neither a registry for these values nor a language-specific indication of the sphere content, so the tokens are treated as opaque strings.

The validity element expresses the rule validity period by two attributes, a starting and an ending time. The validity condition is TRUE if the current time is greater than or equal to at least one from child but less than the until child after it, which represents a logical OR operation across each from and until pair. Times are expressed in XML dateTime format. This mechanism allows invalidating granted permissions automatically without further interaction between the rule maker and the PS; the PS does not remove the rules, so the rule maker has to clean them up. The validity element MUST have the from and until subelements in pairs.
sections.plainLanguage: Three tests are built in: who is asking, what state the person is in, and when the rule applies. Anything else is added by another document. If a test comes from a document the server does not know, the test counts as false.

sections.title: Combining the Permissions of Matching Rules
sections.content:
When a PS receives a request for access to privacy-sensitive data, the request is matched against the rule set. A rule matches if all conditions contained as child elements in the conditions element of a rule evaluate to TRUE. All rules whose conditions match form the matching rule set, and the permissions in the matching rule set are combined using a set of combining rules.

Each type of permission is combined across all matching rules, and each type of action or transformation is combined separately and independently. The combining rules depend only on the data type of the permission. If a particular permission type has no value in a rule, it assumes the lowest possible value for that permission for the purpose of computing the combined permission: FALSE for booleans and the empty set for sets, and any extension to Common Policy must define the equivalent for other data types.

For boolean permissions, the resulting permission is TRUE if and only if at least one permission in the matching rule set has a value of TRUE, and FALSE otherwise. For integer, real-valued and date-time permissions, the resulting permission is the maximum value across the permission values in the matching set of rules. For sets, it is the union of values across the permissions in the matching rule set.

The document's worked example uses two actions, X and Y, of Boolean and Integer type, and a transformation Z whose values can be set to plus or 3, o or 2, or minus or 1, where a value of plus shows the corresponding information unrestricted and minus shows nothing. Six rules are listed with conditions on the requester identity, sphere and validity. The request comes from bob at a time between A1 and A2, with the sphere set to work. Rule 1 does not match on the sphere, rule 2 does not match on the identity, rule 3 matches, rule 4 does not match on the identity, rule 5 matches, and rule 6 does not match because the rule is no longer valid. Only rules 3 and 5 fire. Each column is treated independently: the combined value of X is TRUE, since the missing value equals FALSE; the combined value of Y is 12, the maximum of 3 and 12; and the combined value of Z is o, the maximum of o and minus, that is 2 and 1.
sections.plainLanguage: When several rules match, their permissions are added together: a yes from any rule wins, the largest number wins, and for sets everything is pooled. Each kind of permission is worked out on its own.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document describes a framework for policies, intended to be enhanced elsewhere by application-domain-specific data. Security considerations are to a great extent application-data dependent, and therefore need to be covered by the documents that extend the framework. However, new action and transformation permissions along with their allowed values must be defined in a way so that the usage of the permissions combining rules does not lower the level of privacy protection.

The IANA considerations register a new XML namespace, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:common-policy, a new XML schema at urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:common-policy, and a new MIME type application/auth-policy+xml with the file extension .apxml and intended usage LIMITED USE.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework itself says little about security, because that depends on what the rules are about. The one rule it does set is that anyone adding new permissions must not make the combining rules leak more than before.
